title: Western Ancestors, Part 5: Henry David Thoreau
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The talk's main teaching is that simplicity and non-action can be a powerful path to living fully in the present moment, unencumbered by societal expectations or distractions. Drawing inspiration from Henry David Thoreau's carefree spirit and embodiment of nonviolence, Reizan Bob Penny encourages listeners to cultivate a similar attitude of mindfulness and connection with nature, letting go of external values and dogma to experience reality directly. By embracing this approach, we can find joy and freedom in our daily lives, just as Thoreau did at Walden Pond.

sentences.text: Good evening.
Imagine you have a friend who has decided to leave and go away for a couple of years and live by themselves in a little shack.
You wonder why.
So you send them a letter, and this is what you get back.
*Your question was, what do you do with your time?
There were times when I could not afford to sacrifice the bloom of the present moment to any work, whether of the head or hands.
I love a broad margin to my life.
Sometimes in the summer morning, having taken my accustomed bath, I sat in my sunny doorway from sunrise till noon, wrapped in a reverie amidst the pines and hickories and sumacs.

In undisturbed solitude and stillness, while the birds sang round or flitted noiseless through the house, until by the sun falling in at my west window or the noise of some traveler's wagon on the distant highway, I was reminded of the lapse of time.
I grew in those seasons like corn in the night.*
*And they were far better than any work of the hands would have been.
They were not time subtracted from my life, but so much over and above my usual allowance.
I realized what the orientals mean by contemplation and the forsaking of works.
For the most part, I minded not how the hours went.
The day advanced as if to light some work of mine.
It was morning, and lo, now it is evening, and nothing memorable is accomplished.
Instead of singing like the birds, I silently smiled at my incessant good fortune.*
*As the sparrow had its trill sitting on the hickory before my door, so had I my chuckle or suppressed warble which he might hear out of my nest.
My days were not the days of the week, bearing the stamp of any heathen deity, nor were they minced into hours and fretted by the ticking of a clock.
For I lived like the pure Indians, of whom it is said that for yesterday, today, and tomorrow they have only one word.
And they express the variety of meaning by pointing backward for yesterday, forward for tomorrow, and overhead for the passing day.
This was sheer idleness to my fellow townsman, no doubt.
But if the birds and flowers had tried me by their standard, I should not have been found wanting.
A man must find his occasions in himself, it is true.
The natural day is very calm and will hardly reprove his indolence.*
That's from the chapter entitled "Sounds" from *Walden* by Henry David Thoreau.
I first encountered this book when I was 16, very consciously trying to find some connection between the spiritual life and something I intuited about nature.
By rumor I had it that this book had something to say about it, which it does.
Everyone should read it at some point in their life, especially at a season in their life when they're not sure what to do.
He wrote the book, he said, for poor students.
And he also said that he did not mean to write an ode to dejection, but wanted to brag as lustfully as Chanticleer in the morning, if only to wake up my neighbors.
I've often had this feeling that American nature writing had something to do with the Dharma.

Something about this encounter with what was perceived as a fresh and unspoiled kind of continent might have presented the idea of a true and unveiled connection with nature that wasn't available in the old world.

So that tradition, Thoreau at Walden Pond, Muir going to Yosemite Valley, Abbey in Utah, Dillard at Tinker Creek: these nature writers all had often taken on the guise of an experiment in living as the framework of their encounter.
That seems to be most purely realized in Thoreau's example.

So when we think about Zen hermits in their huts or Tibetan lamas in their caves, we can also think about Henry David and the cabin that he built by himself at Walden Pond, where he lived for two years and wrote a book where he condensed that into the shape of [unclear: "one ear"].
Thoreau was born in 1817.
He graduated from Harvard at age 20, in 1837.
I think that was a normal age, actually, to go through that kind of level of education in those days.
Then he moved back to Concord, Massachusetts, where he lived the rest of his life.
He initially got a job as a schoolteacher, which was pretty short-lived because he was taken to task for refusing to take a student aside and mete out some corporal punishment.
He was so disgusted by that he decided to start a private school with his brother John.

For three years they ran a private school where they did things the way they thought they should do them, like take kids outside and do experiential education and teach them the classics, which is what he had studied at Harvard.
In the middle of that period of teaching private school, he and John took a celebrated boat trip on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers.
He was amongst the crowd of intellectuals growing up during that period who called themselves the transcendentalists.
Concord, being a small place, was actually kind of a center of intellectual discourse.
Ralph Waldo Emerson was his older mentor.
After Thoreau's death, Emerson ended up writing an essay about him in which he says:
*There was somewhat military in his nature, not to be subdued, always manly and able, but rarely tender, as if he did not feel himself except in opposition.
He wanted a fallacy to expose, a blunder to pillory.
I may say required a little sense of victory, a roll of the drum, to call his powers into full exercise.
It cost him nothing to say no.
Indeed, he found it much easier than to say yes.
It seemed as if his first instinct on hearing a proposition was to controvert it, so impatient was he of the limitations of our daily thought.
This habit, of course, is a little chilling to the social affections.
And though the companion would in the end acquit him of any malice or untruth, yet it mars conversation.
Hence no equal companion stood in affectionate relations with one so pure and guileless.
"I love Henry," said one of his friends, "but I cannot like him.
And as for taking his arm, I should as soon think of taking the arm of an elm tree."*
He spent his whole life really doing as little work as possible and never even thinking about the idea of acquiring wealth or property.
Once he thought of buying a farm, but he gave it up.
He contented himself with becoming a land surveyor, which allowed him to do work as he needed.
And also he could get around the countryside, which is what he liked to do.

So he got a reputation of knowing the land and the farms and the woodlots better than their owners, and was often actually brought in to ask about some strange flower or bird or whatnot that nobody else had seen.
He claimed in his later years to have been working on the idea of writing a book where he really cataloged the blooming time of all the plants throughout the year.

He claimed that if he was dropped, as from a spaceship, on the ground, he could tell exactly what day of the year it was based off of knowing the blooming cycle of all the things that were around there.
And he also prided himself on growing a wide variety of [unclear: "melodies"].
But he lived his entire life, outside of those years at Walden, in the upstairs bedroom of the home he grew up in.
We often know about Thoreau via his quotations.
He's very quotable.
He was like the original guy who could write a great sound bite.
So you see his quotes on greeting cards, and this is how we generally know about Thoreau.
People don't read his books, which they should.
But some of the quotes, for instance, that you may have heard:
*Go confidently in the direction of your dreams.
Live the life you have imagined.
It's not what you look at that matters, it's what you see.
Our life is frittered away by detail.
Simplify, simplify.
Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth.
How vain is it to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live?*
*If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost.
That is where they should be.
Now put the foundations under them.*

This quote from *Walden*, which I think is sort of a shadow of the first noble truth: *The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.* So this question, why did he go to [unclear: "Walden Hall"], is something that he actually addressed quite a bit in the beginning of the book, in the chapter entitled "Where I Lived and What I Lived For."
And he says there:

*I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear.
Nor did I wish to practice resignation unless it was quite necessary.
To live deep and suck out all the marrow of life.
To live so sturdily and Spartan-like as to put to rout all that was not life.
To cut a broad swath and shave close.
To drive life into a corner and reduce it to its lowest terms.
And if it proved to be mean, why then get the whole and genuine meanness of it and publish its meanness to the world.*
*Or if it were sublime, to know it by experience and be able to give a true account of it in my next excursion.

For most men, it appears to me, are in a strange uncertainty about it, whether it is of the devil or of God, and have somewhat hastily concluded that it is the chief end of man to glorify God and enjoy him forever.*
So it was as though he was going on [unclear: "his entry"].
He was going to set aside all his preconceptions and address things in their bare essentials.
Now, how does a person come to this sort of state of life where they have acquired this particular attitude and this is what they want to do?
Well, it didn't just come up out of the blue.

He had been, obviously, the person he was, but he had been studying classic texts, he'd been studying Asian religious texts, and he had gone through some personal tragedy, and he was really ready for this.
A few of the transcendentalists, not all of them, had been dabbling in looking at Asian religious texts.

At this point in history, the British East India Society, the Europeans who were doing colonial work in India, had a presence over there and had exposure to texts of Asian origin, mostly coming out of India.
Some people had been doing translation work and had become Sanskritists and [unclear: "quite synologists"].
So there were translations, there were texts, and these made it through the literati circles and the intelligentsia circles into certain inner circles in America.
Emerson started looking at some of these texts in his school days, and it was true that at that time people would look at these as a way to explain how Christianity was the best.
Essentially that was the gist of the study of ancient religions.
They would almost want to set up systems where they saw them in hierarchies piled up.
But it was found that there were common language origins in linguistics, so the idea that the civilizations had common roots was very intriguing to people of that era.
Emerson was reading the Vedas, the Upanishads, and especially the Bhagavad Gita.

But as he became older, and he himself became quite enamored by the teachings in the Asian religions, Emerson wrote in his journal one day, *I owed, my friend and I owed a magnificent day to the Bhagavad Gita.
It was the first of books.
It was as if an empire spake to us.
Nothing small or unworthy, but large, serene, consistent, the voice of an old intelligence which in another age and climate had pondered and thus disposed of the same questions which exercise us.*

Thoreau was not exposed to any Asian text while at Harvard, but soon after coming back to Concord, he was gifted a copy of the Laws of Manu from the epic periods, and he became very enamored with that.
I flipped open my copy of source work in Indian philosophy, [unclear: "so I would probably write to Krishna way back"].
Everybody should own a copy of that.
And I picked out a quote off one of the first lines of the Laws of Manu, which, if you know the Dharmapada, and this predates it by quite a ways, it will be interesting.

*Action, which springs from the mind, from speech, and from the body, produces either good or evil results. [unclear: "The actioner caused"] the various conditions of men, the highest, the middling, and the lowest.*
This was one of Thoreau's prime texts that he was quite interested in.

He sort of was seeing these Asian texts as being confirmative of a kind of karmic yoga, karmic yoga described in the Gita, that allowed him to really authenticate his own experiences, sublime experiences of non-action.

He even wrote to his friend, Harrison Blake, So when he wrote Walden, he began with a long chapter entitled Economy, where he enumerated down to the quarter of a penny the price of every board, nail, brick, bag of rice, sack of beans that he consumed in his entire adventure, and made an exact accounting of it, a sort of economic ledger sheet of his karmic yoga.
But in summing up that whole thing, amid all that accounting, what really comes out of that is that he really seems to want to show how all these physical items support the end use of time.
That was why he really tried to live a life with as little monetary work as possible.
He said, So he seems to be saying that the ways unbarred, almost like a Zen master, the ways unbarred, but it's exactly on the meeting of two eternities.
It's right now.
Improve the nick of time.

About a paragraph later he says that he calls himself the self-appointed inspector of snow storms, and he's a little amiss that the village hasn't appointed him a position and given him money for this.
There's a lot of subtle humor going on.
But his real reason, when it came down to reasons, he says here:

*My purpose in going to Walden Pond was not to live cheaply, nor to live dearly there, but to transact some private business with the fewest obstacles, to be hindered from accomplishing which, for want of a little common sense, a little enterprise and business talent, appeared not so sad as foolish.*

What he was doing was going there to write a book, not Walden, which he wrote later, but a book called A Week on the Concord and Maryknoll Rivers, which was the chronicle of his boat trip with his brother John because just a gear or two before his brother had died in his arms at the lockdown.
It's a lesser known work, but it was closer to his heart.
It's very philosophical.
It's seven chapters divided into a week.
One chapter, he spends almost the entire chapter talking about the Bhagavad Gita.

But he ended up getting that book published, a thousand copies of it, and it sold so poorly that the publisher eventually turned all the remaining copies back over to Thoreau, who claimed in his journal, "I now have a library of nearly 900 volumes, over 700 of which I wrote myself."
He only published a few essays other than those two books in his lifetime, and died young of tuberculosis at age 44.
But his real masterwork was his journal, which went to 33 volumes, 39 volumes actually, which just before his death he built a pinewood coffin for.
He references this in Walden, where he says, "He was long a reporter for a journal of no very wide circulation, whose editor seldom saw fit to print his contributions."
So one day, Henry went out very thick sometimes, and the constable said, "Henry, you haven't paid your poll tax," which is a tax that people had to pay just because they were a person.
And he didn't want to pay this tax because it went to support the Spanish-American War.
And so he got tossed in jail.
Now, he only spent one night there, and somebody, probably a friend at Emerson, sprung him.
He never got to know who.
But he was content to stay there as long as need be.
But as soon as he was let out, he picked up his can and went back up on the hill and started picking berries.
But he ended up writing an essay on the duty of civil disobedience, in which he sounds quite Republican.
"A government which governs the least governs the best."
The well-known lines from that essay.
And this became picked up by Gandhi and Martin Luther King, Jr. as seminal inspiration for their movements of nonviolence.
I actually heard on the radio today that there are some protesters on trial in Snohomish County and environmentalists all over the world apparently are very interested in this case.
They blocked coal train, or not coal train, an oil train.
And they are pleading the necessity argument.
This is the argument that if you break into somebody's house because it's on fire, you're absolved of the crime of breaking in because you did it out of necessity to try and save something.
So their argument is we committed civil disobedience out of the necessity because oil trains are going to kill everybody.
And the judge is allowing this argument to be heard in court.
They're in the third day of testimony on this.
So this is going to be interesting.
This would be an evolution of the legacy of Thoreau.
But one of his works that I think really interests us greatly and interests our mountains and walking practice that we do is his essay, Walking, which is probably his most environmentalist statement.
It was the evolution of two separate essays, one called Walking and one called The Wild.
And he would work up these essays on the lecture circuit, the Lyceum Lecture Circuit, where the society ladies would come.
That's where he would test out the material, refine it, revise it, go through many revisions before it actually went to its printed form.
In this essay, and this is a very often misquoted line, so it's important to get it right, is one of his most famous lines.
But I'll give the little preamble.
He says, and what I have been preparing to say, he says, it's like midway through the essay, that the real point of the whole thing, he says, "in wildness is the preservation of the world."
He believed that things that were wild at their core in any sort of absolute connection to nature was where goodness was.
This, I believe, has something to do with his ability to step outside the thoughts of the religious dogma of his time and to entertain other spiritual notions.
He begins this essay, and if you can imagine him standing up on a lecture, lecturing, and saying this.
This is the beginning word for the essay:

*I wish to speak a word for nature, for absolute freedom and wildness as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil, to regard man as an inhabitant or a part and parcel of nature rather than a member of society.
I wish to make an extreme statement.
If so, I may make an emphatic one for there are enough champions of civilization, the minister and the school committee, and every one of you will take care of that.*

Essentially, he seems to be making a very pointed argument that it's really no great virtue to uphold obvious values, that what we really need to uphold is deep intimacy with true nature, absolute freedom and wildness.
It's a very pure teaching and one that still resonates.
He says in Walden:

*If you stand right fronting face to face with a fact, you will see the sun glimmer on both its surfaces as if it were a scimitar and feel its sweet edge dividing you through the heart and marrow, and so you will happily conclude your moral career, be it life or death, we only crave reality.*
One of the great things that he discusses in the essay is walking, and I find this to be endlessly inspirational for our practice of kinhin, which we rarely contribute much discussion about.
It's just sort of this filler that we do between the sitting, right?
But there's a lot to say about walking.
Thoreau liked to talk about sauntering, and he plays with the word.
He says, where did this word come from?
Did it come from [unclear: "a la saunterere"], to the holy land, he would say, till the children exclaimed, "a saunterer, a holy lander."
And he says, "they who do not go to the holy land in their walks are mere idlers and vagabonds."
But then he also says it could mean sans terre, without land or a home, but equally at home everywhere.
At the end of the essay he says:

*So we saunter toward the holy land, till one day the sun shall shine into our minds and hearts, and light up our whole lives with a great awakening light, as warm and serene and golden as on a bank side in autumn.*
So it seems that there's a lot to learn from viewing Henry David as a Dharma ancestor.
Before even he had moved to Walden Pond, Emerson replaced Margaret Fuller as editor of The Dial, which was the little publication of The Transcendentalists in 1842.
And he began a column, which he enlisted Thoreau to help him with, called Ethnical Scriptures, where they printed some excerpt from world scriptures in every issue.
It was sort of an attempt to eventually create something like a world bible, which was maybe more of a dream of Emerson's to the universalist in him, to see a universal world religion.
But a couple years later, Emerson and Thoreau published in The Dial excerpts from the Lotus Sutra.
It was the first time that Buddhist texts had been published in America.
And they used some of the translations that had come out of Nepal from the British East India Society, gone into French, and they translated the French into English.
So his exposure to Asian religion was not cursory.
It was involved and deep.
And he read the source text and then went and tried to live out some of the realities that he was reading about.
So this passage here I'll read to finish up from Walden.
And after this discussion, maybe you can hear more in this even.
You can hear Dogen in this.
You can hear hard-nosed old Zen teachers.
*Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in.
I drink at it, but while I drink, I see the sandy bottom and detect how shallow it is.
Its thin current slides away, but eternity remains.
I would drink deeper, fish in the sky, whose bottom is pebbly with stars.
I cannot count one.
I know not the first letter of the alphabet.
I've always been regretting that I was not as wise as the day I was born.
The intellect is a cleaver.
It discerns and rifts its way into the secret of things.
I do not wish to be any more busy with my hands than is necessary.
My head is hands and feet.
I feel all my best faculties concentrated in it.
My instinct tells me that my head is an organ for burrowing, as some creatures use their snout and forepaws, and with it I would mine and burrow my way through these hills.
I think that the richest vein is somewhere hereabouts.
So by the dividing rod and thin rising vapors I judge, and here I will begin to mine.*

but equally at home everywhere. At the end of the essay he says, so we saunter toward the holy land, till one day the sun shall shine into our minds and hearts, and light up our whole lives with a great awakening light, as warm and serene and golden

Before even he had moved to Walden Pond, Emerson replaced Margaret Fuller as editor of The Dial, which was the little publication of The Transcendentalists in 1842. And he began a column,

which he enlisted Thoreau to help him with, called Ethnical Scriptures, where they printed some excerpt from world scriptures in every issue. It was sort of an attempt to eventually create something like a world bible, which was maybe more of a dream of Emerson's to the universalist in him,

to see a universal world religion. But a couple years later, Emerson and Thoreau published in The Dial excerpts from the Lotus Sutra. It was the first time that Buddhist texts had been published in America. And they used some of the translations that had come out of Nepal

but while I drink, I see the sandy bottom and detect how shallow it is. Its thin current slides away, but eternity remains. I would drink deeper, fish in the sky, whose bottom is pebbly with stars.

I cannot count one. I know not the first letter of the alphabet. I've always been regretting that I was not as wise as the day I was born. The intellect is a cleaver. It discerns and rifts its way into the secret of things. I do not wish to be any more busy

with my hands than is necessary. My head is hands and feet. I feel all my best faculties concentrated in it. My instinct tells me that my head is an organ for burrowing, as some creatures use their snout and forepaws, and with it I would mine and burrow my way through these hills.
